09_marg269: AND THERE REMAINED. ISIDORE. The younger son, who escapes the sword of the enemy by fleeing, signifies the remnant of Israel, which will believe in the last time and escape the sword of Antichrist. He goes up to the top of mount Garizim, because no one can either prophesy or escape the persecution of Antichrist unless he has first gone up into the mountain of blessing, that is, into the height of faith and virtues. For this is mount Garizim, which was appointed by Moses for blessing.
09_interl467: wandering, unfruitful men, prepared for the eternal burning
09_marg270: THE TREES WENT. ISIDORE. If this deed were not mystical, what need was there to know that Gedeon had seventy sons and many wives, and also a concubine, from whom he had received one son, and a wicked one? Gedeon, then, signified Christ; the wives, the nations which have cleaved to Christ through faith; the seventy sons, the seventy tongues of the world, in which the Lord begot sons for himself through faith; the concubine, the Synagogue, which in the last times will believe in Antichrist, of which it is said: Who say they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan. From it in the last times the wicked son, that is, Antichrist, is to be begotten, the son of the handmaid, that is, of the sinful Synagogue. For whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin. He, gathering the wicked to himself, like Abimelech, will wickedly usurp the kingdom; and, having slain the noble sons, namely the faithful from divers nations and tongues, he will bring in persecution, to kill all the saints.
09_interl468: of the grace of the Holy Ghost
09_marg271: AND THEY SAID TO THE OLIVE TREE: REIGN. ISIDORE. The trees of the forest are unfruitful, vain, wandering men, prepared for the eternal burning. Over these neither the olive nor the fig nor the vine deigns to reign, because they do not deserve it. For the olive signifies the grace of the Holy Ghost and the anointing of peace; the fig the law, which the householder planted in his vineyard: God, namely, who is the father of the household, that is, of all believers; who planted a vineyard, that is, the people of the Jews, and in this vineyard a fig tree, that is, the law; which cast the first people to the ground, like the dry and useless untimely figs, and afterwards brought forth other fruits, that is, the Christian people, which it led with glory and honour to the due ripeness of the evangelical discipline and to the most sweet fatness of Christ.
09_interl470: Christ, who said: "I am the true vine"
09_marg272: And the vine is Christ, who said: "I am the true vine." Because, then, the people which serves Antichrist is given up to a reprobate sense, that it may believe a lie, that is, Antichrist, since it would not believe the truth, that is, Christ, it is rejected from the reign of the vine, that is, of Christ, and from the olive, that is, the grace of the Holy Ghost, and from the fig, that is, the sweetness of the divine law.
09_marg273: AND ALL [THE TREES] SAID. ISIDORE. The bramble is a kind of briar, which is commonly called bear's thorn, very rough and thorny, by which Antichrist is signified, who will lay waste the human race with all roughness and fierceness; and fire shall come out of the bramble, that is, iniquity out of Antichrist, and shall devour all who trust in him together with him.
09_interl472: AUGUSTINE. It is of a more vehement threat, and in a manner of more present efficacy, if one says: If thou wilt not do what I will, let my wrath rage against thee, that is, let it rage now, why do I hold it back? As if he should say: it will rage, threatening future punishment in the manner of a promise.
09_interl473: the faithful of the seventy tongues
09_interl475: the son, namely, of perdition, as you are too
09_interl479: Antichrist himself will destroy both himself and others
09_interl480: ISIDORE. In the persecution of Antichrist none escapes but he who flees and goes up into the mountain of blessing. This is the mountain which the saints surround, which Moses in Deuteronomy appointed for the blessings.
09_marg274: AND THE LORD SENT A SPIRIT. AUGUSTINE. And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of the Sichemites. Whether this word signifies God commanding or permitting cannot easily be determined. For where here is put sent forth, the Greek has exapesteilen, which is also in the Psalm where it is read: "Send forth thy light"; although in some places our translators, where exapesteilen is, have translated sent, not sent forth. It can be understood thus, then: that God sent forth the evil spirit as one willing to go between them, that is, gave power to the evil spirit to disturb their peace. But it is so far from absurd that an evil spirit should even be sent by the Lord for justice' sake, to punish, that some have translated exapesteilen even as sent in.
09_marg275: ARISE THEREFORE IN THE NIGHT. AUGUSTINE. And now arise by night, thou and thy people with thee, and lie in wait in the field; and it shall be in the morning, as soon as the sun riseth, thou shalt make haste and stretch out against the city. Some Latin [codices] have thou shalt make haste [maturabis], some thou shalt rise early [manicabis]. But what the Greek has cannot be said in one word, which is, thou shalt rise at dawn; and perhaps maturabis was said from the morning [matutino] time, although it is also wont to be said at other times for hastening a thing. But manicabis does not occur to me as a Latin word. But this perplexes one, that when it had said, as soon as the sun riseth, it added, thou shalt rise at dawn, since dawn itself, which in Greek is called orthros, signifies the time before the sun, which is now most commonly said when it has begun to grow white. So, then, it is to be understood that what is put as morning is understood as the dawn itself. But as soon as the sun riseth was added to express that it was to be done not when the sun had already risen, but when the brightness of the rising sun appeared. For the dawn grows white from nothing else but when the light of the returning sun has begun to touch the part of the sky which we see in the east. Hence it is that in the Gospel one evangelist says that one and the same thing was done at dawn, while it was yet dark, another at the rising of the sun; because that light of dawn, however little, comes from the sun rising, that is, coming toward its rising, and is known to belong to the sun, casting its brightness from the nearness of its presence. Which light some unlearned men thought was not the sun's, but that which was first created, before God made the sun on the fourth day.
09_marg276: AFTER ABIMELECH. AUGUSTINE. How was a man of the tribe of Issachar the uncle of Abimelech, when Abimelech had as father Gedeon, of the tribe of Manasses? How, then, were Phua and Gedeon brothers, so that Phua could be the uncle of Abimelech, whose son Thola succeeded Abimelech himself? Gedeon and Phua could, then, have had one mother, from whom they were born of different fathers, and been brothers, sons of one mother, not of one father. For women were wont to marry from some tribes into others. Whence Saul too, though he was of the tribe of Benjamin, gave his daughter to David, a man of the tribe of Juda; and a priest of the tribe of Levi married the daughter of king Joram, a man of the tribe of Juda. Hence Elizabeth and Mary are read in the Gospel to be kinswomen, though Elizabeth was of the daughters of Aaron. From which it is understood that some woman of the tribe of Levi married into the tribe of Juda, whence that kinship arose between the two, so that the flesh of the Lord should be propagated not only from the royal but also from the priestly stock.
09_marg277: AUGUSTINE. Jephte is interpreted opening, who signifies Christ. For he opened to his disciples their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures. This Jephte his brethren drove out of their father's house, as sons of a lawful wife [driving out] the son of a harlot. This the chief priests, scribes and Pharisees did against Christ, who seemed to glory in the observance of the law, as though he were undoing the law and therefore were not a lawful son; and as regards the nation, his mother can be called the synagogue of the Jews, which often committed fornication with idols. But they, as observers of the law, seemed lawful, while he seemed to act against the law. Therefore, as lawful sons, they seemed to themselves to have rightly cast out one not lawful: for according to this that people is said to commit fornication, because, not keeping the precepts of the law, it did not show faith as to a husband.
09_interl482: AUGUSTINE. They prevailed, namely, over the weakness of Christ, because he so willed it, that he should suffer at their hands the things he ought. As Jacob too, signifying this same thing, prevailed over the angel, with whom he wrestled that he might foreshow this very thing, the Lord.
09_interl483: AUGUSTINE. as if [they said]: This man is not of God, who keepeth not the sabbath; but boasting themselves to be lawful sons they said: We are not born of fornication; we have one Father, God
09_interl484: AUGUSTINE. Because he hid how great he was, and lay hidden from them in their raging. "For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory." He fled, because they saw the weakness of the dying, but not the power of the rising.
09_marg278: AUGUSTINE. He dwelt in the land of Tob, that is, in the good land, or rather the best. For what in Greek is agathon, in Latin is called best. And Tob is interpreted this, wherein the resurrection seems to be understood. For what land is better than the earthly body clothed with the excellence of immortality and incorruption?
09_marg279: AND THERE WERE GATHERED etc. AUGUSTINE. Before his passion he ate with publicans and sinners, saying: They that are whole need not the physician, but they that are sick. Crucified also among thieves, he carried one of them from the cross into paradise. But after he rose and began to be in the land of Tob, wicked men were gathered to him for the remission of sins, who walked with him, because they lived according to his precepts. This also is done daily, when the ungodly flee to him, that they may be justified and learn his ways.
09_interl485: AUGUSTINE. [Galaad means] casting off, or revelation: because at first they cast Christ off, but afterwards he will be revealed to them.
09_marg280: AUGUSTINE. They who had cast Christ off, turned again to him, received salvation in him. Whence in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter exhorted them to turn to him whom they had persecuted, many were compunct in heart, desiring salvation from him whom they had estranged. For what is to be delivered from enemies but to be saved from sins? For so he says: Do penance, and be baptized every one of you in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins shall be forgiven you. Or rather that calling of the Jews is signified which is hoped for at the end; which seems to be marked when it is said: and it came to pass after days, that is, after a time, as though that is not to be understood which was done when the Lord's passion was recent, but what is to come afterwards. To this seems to pertain that the elders of Galaad came to Jephte, so that by old age the last times are signified.
09_interl486: [Ammon,] which is interpreted 'son of my people' or 'son of sorrow'. These are they who of that very nation remained unbelieving, or who are assigned to hell, or the devil and his angels.
09_interl487: an elegant answer; it expresses the prophecy more evidently
09_interl490: as if: then we came to thee to persecute, now we come to follow.
09_marg281: AND THE PRINCES SAID. AUGUSTINE. Something like this was figured in Joseph, whom his brethren cast off by selling him, and when they were afflicted with famine they turned to his help and mercy. But here the signification of things to come shines out more fully, because not those very brethren who cast out Jephte came to him, but the elders of Galaad, making supplication for the whole people; just as the same nation is called Israel, whether in those who were then and rejected Christ, or in those who afterwards returned to his help. For it is said to a hostile people, whether in its elders or its younger, or in its posterity, drawing out long hatreds and at last converted in those who are then to be converted: Did not you hate me, and cast me out of my father's house? For they thought they had cast Christ out of the house of David, in which "of his kingdom there shall be no end."
09_marg282: AND FIGHT AGAINST THE CHILDREN. AUGUSTINE. That Jephte is sought as leader against the children of Ammon, that when these are conquered they may be delivered, and that they desired to make war under him as leader: since Ammon is interpreted 'son of my people' or 'people of sorrow', either those enemies are signified who of that very nation remained in unbelief, or all who are predestined to hell, where "there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth," as for a people of sorrow; although by the people of sorrow the devil and his angels are fittingly understood, either because they gain eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves are assigned to eternal misery.
09_marg283: I WILL BE YOUR PRINCE. AUGUSTINE. That is, a king, which that nation did not yet have in the time of the Judges. But they began to have Saul as king, and afterwards his successors. For in Deuteronomy, when they are instructed what king they ought to have if it should please them, he is not named there king but prince; but Jephte signified him who is the true king.
09_marg284: AUGUSTINE. A king, namely, as was written in the title of the cross. For after Jephte delivered them from their enemies, he was not made king over them, that we might understand these things to pertain rather to Christ than to Jephte himself, of whom Scripture closes the narrative thus: And Jephte judged Israel six years, and died etc. He judged Israel, then, as the other judges did; he did not reign there as prince, as those did who are contained in the volumes of Kings.
09_interl491: a judge, namely, not a king
09_interl492: because "he is the head of the body, the Church"
09_interl493: AUGUSTINE. He sends messengers of peace, as the Apostle, in whom Christ spoke, says: "If it be possible, as much as is in you, having peace with all men."
09_interl494: AUGUSTINE. The teaching of Christ admonishes us how we are to walk, that is, to live, among those who are not "called to be saints according to his purpose." "For the Lord knoweth who are his."
09_marg285: ARE NOT THOSE THINGS WHICH [HE] POSSESSETH. AUGUSTINE. Shalt thou not possess whatsoever Chamos thy god hath given thee to inherit etc. Which some Latins have translated thus: Shalt thou not possess whatsoever Chamos thy god hath given thee etc. Wherein Jephte seems to have affirmed that the god called Chamos could give some inheritance to his worshippers. But some have it thus: Shalt thou not possess whatsoever Chamos thy god possessed? As though he could possess any such thing. Or perhaps it is said according to this, that the nations are set under angels, according to the canticle of Moses. Is that angel, under whom the children of Ammon were, called Chamos? Who would dare to affirm this, since it can be understood as said according to the opinion of him who thought that his god possessed this, or had given it to him for a possession?
09_interl495: in this it is signified that the Spirit is imparted to the members of Christ
09_interl496: the members of Christ are signified, advancing to carry off the victory over the enemies
09_marg286: AND GOING ROUND GALAAD. AUGUSTINE. Galaad is interpreted 'casting off', Manasses 'necessity of passing over'. There are, then, those casting off, that is, despising, [to be passed over] by those who advance; necessity too is to be passed over, lest perhaps, when he who advances has passed the despisers, he should yield to those who terrify. The watchtower of Galaad also is to be passed over, for Galaad is also interpreted 'revelation'. Now a watchtower is a height for looking forth or looking down, that is, looking from above. The watchtower of Galaad, then, seems to signify pride of revelation; whence: "And lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me" etc. Therefore this too is to be passed over, that is, one must not remain in it, because of the danger of falling. These being passed, the enemies are easily overcome; which it signifies by saying, and passing from the watchtower of Galaad, and passing over to the children of Ammon.
09_marg287: IF THOU WILT DELIVER THE CHILDREN OF AMMON. AUGUSTINE. Whomever he had in mind, Jephte does not seem to have had his daughter in mind. For he would not say: Alas, my daughter, thou hast hindered me etc. For he shows that he was hindered from fulfilling what he had had in mind. But whom could he have in mind, who had no sons? Or did he have his wife in mind, and God did not will this to be done, and [so it came about] that he should not leave [the vow] unpunished, lest anyone afterwards should dare it; and that by great providence, from what befell, a great sacrament of the Church should be figured? From both, then, the prophecy was fitted: namely from what he had in mind in vowing, and from what befell him against his will. For if he had his wife in mind, the wife of Christ is the Church. But because the wife of this Jephte could not be a virgin, in that his daughter rather met him, both the rashness of the vow did not remain unpunished and the virginity of the Church was figured. To whom it is said: Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace.
09_marg288: WHOSOEVER SHALL FIRST. AUGUSTINE. Concerning the daughter of Jephte there is wont to be a great question for some who piously seek and desire to know what it means; for some who oppose the Scriptures with unskilled impiety, it is a charge, that the God of the law and the prophets delights even in human sacrifices. But neither did those sacrifices delight him in which holocausts of cattle were offered. But because they were significative, and certain shadows of things to come, he wished to commend to us the things signified by these sacrifices. And this also was a useful reason why they were changed and are now not only not commanded but forbidden to be offered: lest we should think that God truly delights in such things according to carnal affection.
09_marg289: But whether it was fitting that things to come should be signified even by human sacrifices is rightly asked: not that we ought in this matter to shudder at the deaths of men who must die at some time, but that those who would gladly accept this being done to themselves might be commended to God for an eternal reward. But if this were true, this sacrifice would not displease God. Yet Scripture testifies that it displeases him. For though he willed and commanded all firstborn to be his, yet he willed the firstborn of men to be redeemed from him, lest they should believe that their firstborn were to be immolated to God. Whence: Thou shalt not do in like manner to the Lord thy God; for they have done to their gods all the abominations which the Lord hateth, when they burned their sons and daughters with fire to their gods. Not only, then, does God not love, but he even hates such sacrifices, in which men are immolated. But those he loves and crowns, when the just man contends for the truth even unto death, or is slain by enemies whom he has offended for justice' sake, rendering them good for evil, that is, love for hatred. Such, he says, is the just blood, from the blood of Abel unto the blood of Zacharias. But chiefly, that he himself shed his blood for us and offered himself a sacrifice to God; and so he offered it, that he was slain by enemies for justice' sake. Imitating him, the martyrs contended even unto death for the truth, of whom it is said: As gold in the furnace he hath proved them, and as a victim of a holocaust he hath received them. Whence the Apostle: For I am even now ready to be sacrificed. But not as Jephte immolated his daughter to the Lord, but as it was commanded that cattle be offered, and forbidden that men be immolated. This seems more like that which Abraham did, which the Lord specially commanded to be done; not generally did he ever command such sacrifices to be made to himself, nay, he forbade them altogether to be made. What Jephte did, then, differs from the deed of Abraham, because the one offered his son at command, the other did what is forbidden by the law and is enjoined by no special command. In the very son of Abraham too the Lord showed that he did not delight in such sacrifices, when he forbade the father, whose faith he had proved by commanding, to slay his son, and set by a ram, by which the sacrifice might lawfully be completed according to the custom fitting the time.
09_marg290: But if this moves anyone, how Abraham piously believed that God delights in such sacrifices, if they are offered unlawfully, and he therefore thinks that Jephte too rightly believed that such a sacrifice could be acceptable to God: first let him consider that it is one thing to vow of one's own accord, another to obey one who commands. For if something to his loss, beyond custom, is commanded a servant by his lord, and he does it with praiseworthy obedience, it does not follow that he is not to be punished if he has presumed to do it of his own accord. Then Abraham had ground to believe that [it was] beyond the divine command [that he] not spare his son, not believing that God gladly accepts such victims, but that he had commanded it in order to raise up the slain, and thereby, as a wise God, to show something. Whence his faith is praised in the Epistle to the Hebrews, because he believed this of God, that he could raise up his son. But this man, God neither commanding nor demanding it, and against the lawful precept of God, of his own accord vowed a human sacrifice. For he says: Whosoever shall come forth from the doors of my house to meet me etc. In these words he did not vow some beast which could be offered according to the law. Nor was it the custom that cattle should come to meet leaders returning with victory. Dogs indeed are wont to run to meet their masters; of these, since he did not vow them, he could not have thought, lest he seem to have vowed, to God's injury, a thing not only unlawful but also contemptible and unclean according to the law. Nor does he say 'Whatsoever shall come forth' but 'Whosoever shall come forth', where he had only a man in mind. Not, however, perhaps his only daughter, though who could go before her in so great glory of her father, unless perhaps his wife? For as to his saying not 'whosoever' [in the feminine] but whosoever [in the masculine] shall come forth from the doors of my house, Scripture is wont to put the masculine gender for either sex, as it was said of Abraham: Rising up from his dead, when his wife had died.
09_marg291: Since, then, Scripture seems to have passed no judgment on this vow and deed, as on Abraham when at command he offered his son, but only to have left it written for readers to judge; as with the deed of Juda, when he went in to his daughter-in-law, unknowing indeed, but as far as in him lay he committed fornication, because he thought her a harlot, and Scripture neither approved this nor reproved it, but left it to be weighed by consulting the justice and law of God: so concerning the deed of Jephte it gave sentence on neither side, that our understanding might be exercised in judging. We might now say that such a vow displeased God, and that it was brought to that vengeance, that his only daughter above all should meet her father. For if he had hoped and willed this, he would not, on seeing her, at once have rent his garments and said: Alas, thou hast hindered me, my daughter etc. Then, so long a delay of sixty days being given to his daughter, the Lord did not forbid him the death of his only and dearest one, as he did Abraham, until by performing it he bereaved himself, but did not appease God by the immolation of a human being; and therefore this penalty was rendered to the father, lest the example of such a vow be left unpunished, so that men should either think they vowed some great thing to God when they vowed human victims, and, what is more horrible, those of their children; or those same vows should be not true but rather feigned, since, as by the example of Abraham, they would hope, knowing that God would forbid such vows to be fulfilled. We might, I say, say this, unless two testimonies of the Scriptures held us back, that we should search diligently into this deed, committed to memory in books of so great authority, lest we judge rashly. One, that Jephte is mentioned among such men that we should fear to blame him, when it is said: For the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, Barac, Samson, Jephte etc. The other, that Scripture set first, saying: And the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephte etc. And added: And Jephte vowed a vow to the Lord etc., so that all the things that were done afterwards seem to be understood as works of the spirit of the Lord which came upon him.
09_marg292: AUGUSTINE. But among praiseworthy men is not only Jephte but also Gedeon, of whom Scripture likewise says: The spirit of the Lord strengthened Gedeon etc.; that he made an ephod we not only do not approve, but openly, Scripture judging it, reprove. Nor yet is any injury done to the spirit of the Lord, who strengthened him. Yet he is mentioned among those who by faith conquered kingdoms, wrought justice; because holy Scripture, whose faith and justice it truly praises, is not hindered from noting their sins. For in this too, that Gedeon, asking a sign, as he spoke, made trial with the fleece, I know not whether he did not transgress this precept: Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. But yet even in his trial the Lord showed what he wished to foretell; nor was it in vain that among the faithful and those working justice he merited such testimony, for the good and faithful life in which it is to be believed he died.
09_marg293: But whether, because after it was said: The spirit of the Lord came upon Jephte, these things followed, that he vowed that vow and conquered the enemies and paid the vow, all are to be ascribed to the spirit of the Lord, so that this sacrifice too should be held as if the Lord had commanded it, as to Abraham, I would not easily say, since after Gedeon made the ephod no prosperity is recorded. But after Jephte vowed the vow, his victory followed, for which he had vowed, and having obtained it, he paid the vow. For again it is to be considered that Gedeon, though not after he made the ephod, yet after he tempted the Lord (which is certainly a sin), with great slaughter of the enemies overcome, gained salvation for the people. For thus it is written: And Gedeon said to the Lord: Let not thy wrath be kindled against me, if I try once more in the fleece. For he feared the wrath of God, because he knew that he sinned in tempting, which God manifestly forbids in his law. Yet this sin was followed both by the evidence of a wonderful sign and by the prosperity of victory. For God had already determined to succour the afflicted people, and he used the mind of this leader whom he had taken for this work, not only faithful and pious but also failing and offending, both to foretell what he willed and to fulfil what he had said.
09_marg294: For not only through these, who, though they sinned, are reckoned among the just, but also through Saul, wholly reprobate, God bestowed many things on his people; upon whom also the spirit of the Lord leapt, and he prophesied. For he did not know how to act justly, in that, namely, he raged against David, a holy man. The spirit of the Lord works through the good and the bad, through the knowing and the unknowing, what he knows and has determined is to be done; who also through Caiphas, not knowing what he said, prophesied that Christ must die for the nation.
09_marg295: For who did it but the spirit of the Lord, caring to foretell things to come, that it should come into the mind of Gedeon, wishing to tempt the Lord and not believing what the Lord had already spoken to him, [to ask] this above all, of the fleece first wet with rain then dry, and of the floor first dry then watered? So that what falls short in faith may be ascribed to his offence; but that God used such a mind of his is to be left to his mercy and wonderful providence.
09_marg296: But if anyone says that Gedeon did and said all things knowingly by prophetic revelation, that through him such signs might be shown, and that he did not fail in faith, and believed what the Lord had already promised him, but by a prophetic action willed to make trial in the fleece, and that therefore the trial was blameless, like the guile of Jacob; and that what he said to the Lord: Let not thy wrath be kindled against me, he did not say because he feared wrath, but because he trusted that he would not be angry, since he was doing what he perceived was to be done at the Spirit's dictation: let him say as it seems [to him], provided that he does not dare to excuse from sin the deed of the ephod which Scripture blamed, whatever it may signify.
09_marg297: For that, too, the three hundred men, pertaining by their very number to the sign of the cross, took earthen pitchers and shut burning torches in them, which being broken, the lights suddenly terrified the multitude of the enemies, Gedeon seems to have done as of his own will. For Scripture does not say that the Lord moved him to do it; and yet so great a sign, who but the Lord inspired to be done? He prefigured that the saints would have the treasure of the evangelical light in earthen vessels. Whence: We have this treasure in earthen vessels; which being broken in their passion, a greater brightness of their glory shone forth, which overcame the enemies by the unlooked-for brightness of Christ.
09_marg298: Whether, then, through the knowing or through the unknowing, the spirit of the Lord wrought the signification of things to come in prophetic times. Nor were their sins therefore not sins; because God, who uses even evil things well, used them to signify what he willed.
09_marg299: If, then, it was not a sin either to vow or to pay a sacrifice of any human death, or even a parricidal one, because it signified something great and spiritual, in vain did God forbid such things and say that he hates them, since even those things which he commanded to be done are referred to the signification of spiritual things. But human sacrifices did not please God, when one is slain not for justice, as one who lives rightly or will not sin, but a man is immolated by a man like a chosen victim, in the manner of cattle.
09_marg300: But if anyone says that, because the victims of cattle, now customary, though referred to a signification, made men less intent on seeking the great sacrament of Christ and the Church, God therefore, wishing to rouse the minds of men by a notable and unlooked-for thing, the more so because he had forbidden such sacrifices to be offered to him, took care that something be offered to him in which the very wonder should beget a great question, and the question should demand study to search out the mystery; and that the mind of man, piously searching the depth of the prophecy, should draw up Christ, as a fish with a hook, from the deep of the Scriptures: to this reasoning we do not object. But it is one question concerning the mind of the one vowing, another concerning the providence of God, who uses most well a mind of whatever kind.
09_marg301: [If] therefore the spirit of the Lord, which came upon Jephte, commanded him to vow this, which Scripture has not disclosed, whose commands it is not lawful to despise, not only is folly not to be blamed, but obedience to be praised.
09_marg302: For in this way, even if a man should kill himself, which it is wicked to do by human will and counsel, it is to be understood to be done obediently, not wickedly.
09_marg303: But if Jephte, following a human error, thought a human sacrifice should be vowed, his sin indeed was justly punished in his only daughter, which he himself seems to show, rending his garments and saying: Alas, my daughter, thou hast hindered me etc.
09_marg304: Yet this error has some praise of faith, because he feared God, so as to pay what he had vowed, and did not decline the sentence of the divine judgment upon himself: whether hoping that the Lord would forbid it, as he did to Abraham, or resolving to do his will, understood even when he did not forbid, rather than to despise it.
09_marg305: Although here it is rightly asked whether it is more truly understood that God did not will this to be done, and that God would rather be obeyed in it if it were not done, since he had shown that he did not will this, both in the son of Abraham and in the lawful prohibition. But yet, if Jephte did not do it for that reason, he would seem rather to have spared himself in his only daughter than to have followed the will of God. He rather understood, then, in that his daughter met him, God as avenger, and faithfully submitted himself to just punishment, fearing a fiercer vengeance for evasion. For he believed that the soul of his good and virgin daughter was well received, because she did not vow herself to be immolated, but had not resisted her father's vow and will and had followed the judgment of God. For death, as it is not to be inflicted on oneself by anyone of his own accord, nor on anyone else of one's own accord, so when God commands it is not to be refused, by whose ordinance it must be undergone at some time. Nor does anyone who shrinks from suffering it labour to avoid it altogether, but only to put it off.
09_marg306: ISIDORE. Jephte signifies Christ, who, departing from the face of his brethren, that is, the Jews, received the princedom among the Gentiles; because he fulfilled all the sacraments of human salvation as one sworn, and offered his own flesh, as a daughter, for the salvation of Israel. And he swore to the Father and vowed, according to that: "How he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob": namely that he would fulfil the sacrament of religion in the passion of his flesh for the salvation of the human race. These things, then, were so done by Christ that they seem to be fulfilled by the religion of an oath.
09_marg307: AND MAY BEWAIL MY VIRGINITY. AUGUSTINE. The chaste virgin, that is, the Church, will become a holocaust in the resurrection, when in her entire that will be done which is written: "Death is swallowed up in victory." Then the true Jephte will deliver the kingdom, that is, the Church, to God and the Father, when the sixth age of the world is completed; therefore a delay of sixty days was asked. For the Church is gathered out of all the ages: namely from Adam to the flood, from the flood, that is, from Noe, to Abraham; thence to David; then to the transmigration of Babylon; from the transmigration to Christ; thence to the end of the world. Through these six ages, as through sixty days, the holy virgin weeps her virginity; because, though virginal, yet there were sins to be bewailed. Whence through the whole world she cries: "Forgive us our debts, etc." These sixty days she preferred to call two months, because of the two men: one through whom came death, the other through whom came the resurrection of the dead; because of whom also two testaments are spoken of.
09_interl497: AUGUSTINE. Sixty days, that is, the six ages in which the virgin Church is gathered and laments her sins, saying daily: "Forgive us our debts."
09_interl499: Christ, whose daughter is the Church
09_interl500: delivering, namely, the kingdom to God and the Father
09_interl501: "I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ"
09_marg308: FROM THENCE CAME A FASHION. AUGUSTINE. But as to what was done by precept in Israel, that from days to days they assembled to lament the daughter of Jephte four days in the year, I do not think it signifies anything after the holocaust is fulfilled, which will be in eternal life, but the past times of the Church, in which the mourners were blessed. By the four days its universality is figured, because of the four parts of the world through which it is spread far and wide. But as to the proper sense of the history, I do not think the Israelites decreed this, except because they understood that in this matter the judgment of God was shown rather to strike the father, lest anyone thereafter should vow such a sacrifice. For why was lamentation decreed, if that vow was a matter of joy?
09_interl502: signifying the past times of the Church, in which "Blessed are they that mourn."
09_interl503: because of the four parts of the world through which the Church is spread
09_interl504: This is to be referred to the last judgment, according to that: "Those that would not have me reign over them, bring hither, and kill them before me."
09_marg309: AND HE JUDGED. As those two months, because of the sixty days, signify the number six of the six ages, so here six times seven multiplied figures this same thing, as far as pertains to the six ages of the world. For six times seven are forty-two; nor was it in vain that Jephte himself judged the people six years.
09_marg310: NOW THERE WAS A CERTAIN MAN. ISIDORE. Samson has certain things in type of Christ: namely, that his birth is announced by an angel. For thus the angel of the Lord said to the Virgin: "Mary, thou hast found grace with God. Behold thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and shalt bring forth a son" etc. Samson also is called a Nazarite, and of Christ it was said that he shall be called a Nazarene. Samson delivered the children of Israel from the hand of the enemies, and Christ his people from their sins. Samson is interpreted their sun, and of Christ it was said by the Prophet: Unto you the sun of justice shall arise, and health in his wings.
09_marg311: NOR ANY UNCLEAN THING. AUGUSTINE. The unclean thing is the loosening of discipline which had begun to be in Israel, and had already brought them down to eating those things which God had forbidden among the animals. For they were already passing over even to the worship of idols.
09_interl507: AUGUSTINE. This Scripture passed over in silence above
09_marg312: AND WHEN SHE WAS COME. AUGUSTINE. What the woman says was told her by the angel, that the child shall be a Nazarite of God from the womb until the day of his death, is not read as said by the angel; and what is read as said, He shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines, is not mentioned by the woman. She did not, then, tell something that she heard; and yet she is to be believed to have told nothing that she did not hear. But rather Scripture did not set down all the words of the angel when it brought him in speaking to the woman. And it was said, From the womb until the day of his death, for this reason: because those were called Nazarites in the law for a time who had a vow, according to what Scripture had commanded by Moses. Hence it is that this was commanded him, that iron should not come upon his head, and that he should not drink wine and strong drink: for these Samson kept all his life, which those who were called Nazarites observed for certain days, vowing and paying the vow.
09_marg313: THEN MANUE TOOK. AUGUSTINE. From what Scripture says, that Manue did not know that it was the angel of the Lord, it is manifest that his wife too believed him a man. When, then, he said to him: Let us now constrain thee, and make ready in thy sight a kid of the goats, he invited him as a man, namely that he might feast with him on what he had made a sacrifice. For to make a kid is not wont to be said except when a sacrifice is made. He too so answered: If thou constrain me, I will not eat of thy bread; where he shows that he had been invited to a feast. Then he added: And if thou wilt make a holocaust, offer it to the Lord; because, namely, he had said: Let us make ready in thy sight a kid of the goats. But not every sacrifice is a holocaust: for of a holocaust nothing was eaten, because the whole was burnt, and therefore it was called a holocaust. But the angel, not being about to eat, advised that a holocaust rather be made, yet not to himself but to the Lord: because, namely, Israel at that time had been accustomed to sacrifice to false gods. Whence too it had then offended God, so as to be delivered to enemies for forty years.
09_marg314: AND WHEN [MANUE] SAW THIS. GREGORY. What is it that at the vision of the angel the man is fearful, the woman bold, except that when heavenly things are shown to us, the spirit indeed shakes itself with dread, but yet hope is confident? For hope raises itself to see greater things from that very thing by which the spirit is troubled, which sees first the things that are above; because when the mind, thus lifted up, beholds the higher things of the heavenly secrets, all the firmness of human strength trembles.
09_marg315: WE SHALL CERTAINLY DIE. AUGUSTINE. What is it that, after the angel who was speaking with them was made manifest to Manue and his wife, Manue said to his wife: We shall die the death etc.? Because, namely, of what is written: No man can see my face and live. They thought, then, as men, that they had seen God, so great a miracle having been done, that he stood in the fire of the sacrifice who before had spoken with them as a man. But did they call God in the angel, or the angel himself God? For thus it is written: And Manue took a kid of the goats, and made a sacrifice, and offered it upon a rock to the Lord who doth wonderful things, and Manue and his wife looked on etc. From these words, then, because he did not say: We shall die the death because we have seen the angel of the Lord, but, We have seen God, the question arises: whether they understood God in the angel, or called the same angel God? For that third [possibility], that they had thought him God who was an angel, cannot be said, since Scripture openly says: Then he knew that it was the angel of the Lord. But whence did they fear death? For it was not written: No man seeth the face of an angel and shall live. Or was Manue, in this very thing, that he had known God in the presence of the angel, so troubled that he feared death? But as to what his wife answered him: If the Lord would kill us, he would not have received holocausts and sacrifice at our hand, nor have shown all these things, nor have done these things for us as we heard: did they believe that the angel himself had received the sacrifice, because they saw him stand in the flame of the altar? Or did they understand by this that the Lord had received it, because the angel did this to show himself an angel? Whichever of these it be, the angel had already said: But if thou make a holocaust, offer it to the Lord, that is: not to me but to the Lord. That the angel stood in the flame of the altar, then, is rather to be understood as having signified that the angel of great counsel, in the form of a servant, that is, in the man whom he was to take up, would not receive a sacrifice, but would himself be the sacrifice.
09_marg316: THEN [SAMSON] WENT DOWN. ISIDORE. Samson, when he went to the foreigners for the sake of seeking a wife, slew a lion; and Christ, about to call his Church from the Gentiles, overcame the devil, who says: Rejoice, for I have overcome the world. From the mouth of the slain lion the honeycomb is drawn, because, as we behold, the kings of the earthly kingdom who before had raged against Christ, their fierceness now destroyed, proclaim the sweetness of the Gospel and furnish it defences.
09_marg317: AND HE MADE A GREAT SLAUGHTER OF THEM. THE SEVENTY. Samson smote the foreigners leg upon thigh: that is, so wonderfully that in astonishment they laid the leg of one foot upon the thigh of the other.
09_marg318: SWEAR, HE SAID. AUGUSTINE. What is it that Samson says to the men of Juda: Swear to me that you will not kill me, and deliver me to them, lest perhaps you fall upon me? Which expression some have translated thus: lest perhaps you come against me. But that he said this lest he be killed by them is shown by what is written in the book of Kings, when Solomon commanded that a man be killed, saying: Go, fall upon him. Which is not understood for this reason, that it is not our custom so to speak. For so what the military authorities say: Go, lift him up, and it means 'kill him', who would understand, except one who knew the custom of that expression? It is also commonly said among us: compendiavit illi ['he cut him short'], that is, he killed him; and no one understands this except one who has been used to hearing it. For this is the general force of all expressions: that as languages themselves are not understood unless they are learned by hearing or reading, so neither are the modes of expression.

09_marg319: WITH THE JAWBONE. GREGORY. The jawbone of the ass signifies preachers. For our Redeemer, holding in the hand of his power the simplicity and patience of the preachers, slew the carnal [to free them] from vices; and the jawbone, cast to the ground, afterwards poured forth waters, because the bodies of the preachers, given over to death, showed great miracles to the peoples.
09_interl511: because, after the bodies of the preachers died, they showed great miracles
09_marg320: AND HE JUDGED. GREGORY. Whom does Samson signify in this deed but the Redeemer? What is Gaza but hell? What the Philistines but the faithlessness of the Jews? Who, when they saw the Lord dead, and his body laid in the sepulchre, at once appointed guards, and rejoiced that the author of life was held by the bars of hell, as though they had caught Samson in Gaza. But Samson at midnight not only went out but also carried off the gates; because our Redeemer, rising before the light, not only went out free from hell, but also destroyed the bars of hell. He carried off the gates and went up to the top of the hill, because by rising he took away the bars of hell, and by ascending he entered the kingdom of heaven.

09_marg321: AND SHE CALLED A BARBER. ISIDORE. That the crafty woman shaved Samson's head and gave him over to the Allophyli to be mocked, that he was taken captive, that he was blinded and appointed to the mill: in these not Christ but those are figured who only glory in the name of Christ and are continually entangled in evil deeds. For the man is understood as the rational sense; but the woman signifies the flesh. For if we consent to the woman, that is, to our flesh, when lust flatters, or to other evil works, we are stripped bare of the grace of the Holy Ghost, which is signified by the Nazarite's hair, and are deceived. For thus, the grace of Christ being violated, the proud and sinners are mocked by the devil, as Samson was when his hair was cut. But if anyone returns by doing penance, his hair returning, that is, grace flowering again, he is restored to strength, and, the pillars of covetousness and lust being overthrown, he has cast down the enemies, and, the combat renewed, he will triumph most mightily over the demons unto the end.
09_marg322: AND WHEN [THEY] HAD SEIZED HIM. GREGORY. Samson, having lost his eyes, is appointed by the Allophyli to the mill. It is to be known that first the understanding is dulled, and afterwards the captive mind wanders through outward desires, so that the blind mind knows not whither it is led and willingly submits itself to the allurements of the flesh. But sometimes the desires of the flesh first boil up, and after long use close the eye of the heart by unlawful works. For often the mind discerns rightly, and yet does not boldly raise itself against perverse things, and, struggling, is overcome, while, judging the very thing it did, it is overpowered by the delight of its flesh. For that most often the eye of contemplation is first lost, and afterwards through the desires of the flesh the mind is subjugated to the labours of this world, Samson witnesses, taken by the Allophyli, who after he lost his eyes was appointed to the mill; because the malignant spirits, after they have dug out the keenness of contemplation within by the goads of temptations, send [the mind] outside into the round of labour.
09_marg323: AND MANY MORE. GREGORY. In this place Christ is signified by Samson. For Samson, while he lived, slew few; but in overthrowing the temple, dying, he slew a very great multitude of adversaries; and when our Lord preached, few of the Jews believed, but innumerable peoples of the Gentiles followed the way of life when he died. For the proud he bore with while he still lived subject to suffering; but having died [and risen] to impassible life, he laid them low. This Samson long ago expressed figuratively in himself, who slew few while he lived, but, the temple being destroyed, killed many when he died: because the Lord extinguished few from the loftiness of pride while he lived, more when the temple of his body was dissolved; and the chosen [so the edition] from the Gentiles, whom he bore with by living, he laid low all together by dying.
09_marg324: AND THEY CONSULTED. GREGORY. He who does not judge himself does not know what he may rightly judge in another. Even if perhaps he knows by hearing how he ought to judge rightly, yet he cannot rightly judge the merits of others, to whom the conscience of his own innocence affords no rule of judgment. Hence it is that when the tribe of Benjamin had been overwhelmed in a crime of the flesh, all Israel, gathered together, wished to avenge the iniquity, and yet was laid low in battle once and again. But when [the Lord] was consulted whether they ought to go to avenge it, it was commanded. Israel, which went on according to the command of the divine voice, lost once and a second time, and at last almost utterly destroyed the sinning tribe. What is it, then, that they are inflamed to avenge the crime and are first laid low, except that those by whom the faults of others are struck must first themselves be purged, so that those who hasten to correct the vices of others may come to the vengeance already clean? Whence: "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." For they were going to punish the sins of others, and had left their own. They are called back, then, to conscience, that they may first correct their own and then reprove those of others. Whence it is necessary that, while the divine vengeance ceases against us, conscience itself should reprove itself and raise itself against itself to the laments of penance, lest it be lifted up against the good and humble [so the edition] toward itself; but let it be rigid against itself, and submissive to all the good.
